newsitem.title: GREECE: PRESS DIGEST - GREEK GENERAL NEWS- NOV 13.
newsitem.headline: PRESS DIGEST - GREEK GENERAL NEWS- NOV 13.

text.p: Leading stories in the Greek general press:
KATHIMERINI

--Differing positions on the economic policy the government should follow were aired at yesterday's marathon informal inner cabinet meeting, chaired by Prime Minister Costas Simitis. The dissension was a precursor to the difficulties the government is expecting in applying its chosen policy. The Cabinet meeting expected to give the final seal of approval to the 1997 budget has been moved from tomorrow to next Tuesday, following Monday's meeting of PASOK MPs and party Central Committee on the same issue.

--The Athens Stock Exchange will resume trading today, brokers say, following their approval of a compromise solution worked out by the national economy ministry. Prosecutors, meanwhile, have filed charges against unnamed persons for negligence in the light of the scandal that kept the bourse shut for three days.

--Municipalities and local government bodies in the Attica prefecture begin their four-day closure tomorrow, calculated to get the government to change its mind about a 25 percent reduction in their revenues.

--An agreement on the issue of extended trading hours appears likely as merchants, employees and the commerce ministry meets today. Reports say stores will extend trading hours to 4 or 5 p.m. on Saturday.
ELEFTHEROTYPIA
--Reports state that the government's new tax on large real estate holdings and the abolition of tax breaks and relief will be applied retroactively for 1996.

--A prophetic report from the members of the Capital Market Commission issued 18 months ago had warned of the likelihood of problems on the stock exchange. Efforts now are being focused on salvaging the bourse's reputation although the problems still remain.
--Alternate Foreign Minister George Papandreou enters the debate on heavier penalties for drug use, saying he is in favour of the decriminalisation of cannabis.

--Sophia Papandreou-Katsanevas, the daughter of late ruling party PASOK founder and president Andreas Papandreou, urges prosecutors to continue examining rumours her ailing father was treated with homeopathic medicines without the knowledge of his physician.
--As the weekend's 23nd anniversary of the 1973 Polytechnic uprising approaches, students and teachers up the ante with new protests, strikes and occupations. TA NEA

--The government's proposed tax exemptions abolition bill is to be tabled in Parliament after the budget, to offset adverse reaction. Yesterday's inner cabinet saw disagreement on how to tax low pension earners and the level of wage increases for public servants.
ELEFTHEROS TYPOS
--European Union Commissioner Christos Papoutsis says that Greece needs to be more definite on its strategy on Greek-Turkish relations.
--The government comes in for a hiding in Parliament yesterday with opposition and four PASOK MPs lashing out at the wage increases for security forces and the military as inadequate.
--The European Court decides that member-states have the right to declare Sunday a working day.
ETHNOS

--After arguing for five hours, the inner cabinet yesterday decided only on 17 measures, including taxation of state titles, mutual funds, banks, donations and property. Journalists, MPs, prefects, mayors and pilots lose their tax breaks.

--The Turkish 'Flexible Pincer' naval exercise has closed off the region between the islands of Chios and Lesvos and means that Greek fighter planes cannot communicate with the islands. --Maria Petrakis, Athens Newsroom +301 3311812-4
